title: Commas and brackets for clear meaning

steps.say: Use commas to separate items in a list. The last two items are joined by and.
Put a comma after a fronted adverbial or an opening clause.
Put commas around extra information in the middle of a sentence.
steps.show: Pak Joko, our gardener, grows chillies.

steps.say: Brackets can also hold extra information. The sentence must make sense without it.
A comma in the right place can change the meaning, so read your sentence aloud.

options.text: My brother (who is six loves dinosaurs).
options.why: The brackets should close after six.

options.text: My brother (who is six) loves dinosaurs.
(My brother) who is six loves dinosaurs.
options.why: My brother is the main subject, so it should not be in brackets.

options.text: My (brother who is six) loves dinosaurs.
options.why: The brackets should hold only the extra information.

hints: Read each sentence without the bracketed words. Does it still make sense?
Find the extra information first: how old is the brother?
check.explanation: Who is six is extra information, so it goes in brackets. My brother loves dinosaurs still makes sense without it.

check.prompt: A comma is missing. Write the word that the comma should come after. Before the bell rang we packed our bags.
hints: The sentence starts with a subordinate clause.
The comma goes where the opening clause ends.
Find the main clause: who packed their bags?
check.explanation: Before the bell rang is the opening clause, so the comma comes after rang.
